title: Irish activist indicted in US over alleged destruction of $60M military plane
text:
The $60 million U.S. military aircraft was damaged beyond repair and will never fly again, federal prosecutors said

Anti-Israel activist faces federal charges after military aircraft destroyed

Fox News national correspondent Bryan Llenas joins 'America Reports' to discuss how federal prosecutors charged an anti-Israel activist after a $60 million U.S. Air Force warplane was destroyed and deemed a total loss in New York.

An Irish anti-Israel activist was indicted in the United States after allegedly destroying a $60 million American military aircraft at an airport in Ireland, leaving the plane damaged beyond repair after what prosecutors described as months of meticulous planning.

Federal prosecutors announced the indictment Tuesday, seven months after Daithi O'Corrain, 48, allegedly breached the security perimeter at Shannon Airport in western Ireland and broke into an unoccupied U.S. Air National Guard C-130H Hercules aircraft.

Prosecutors said O'Corrain then spent hours damaging the aircraft, cutting critical wiring and hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit instruments, puncturing air ducts and pinching shut the aircraft's liquid oxygen line.

2 FOREIGN NATIONALS BREACH UK BASE HOUSING KEY US, NATO INTEL HUB AMID $556M EXPANSION

Left: Smashed cockpit instruments inside a U.S. military C-130H Hercules aircraft allegedly destroyed at Shannon Airport in Ireland April 11, 2026. Right: A separate U.S. Air Force C-130 Hercules aircraft at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, England, March 18, 2026. (U.S. Department of Justice; Leon Neal/Getty Images )

The damage was so extensive it rendered the aircraft inoperable, and the $60 million plane will never return to active flight status, according to federal authorities.

Photographs released by federal prosecutors show extensive damage inside the aircraft, including smashed cockpit instruments, severed wiring and damaged equipment. Other images show tools allegedly used in the attack and O'Corrain standing on the aircraft's roof before his arrest.

Months of planning

According to the indictment, O'Corrain spent months researching the aircraft's construction, acquiring tools and gallium, a metal capable of corroding aluminum, and using a flight-tracking app to monitor military aircraft. He also researched previous attacks on U.S. military planes at Shannon Airport and searched for locations where he could breach the airport's security perimeter.

O'Corrain, who also goes by the name David Curran and is from County Cork in southern Ireland, was charged with destruction of government property, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

FBI Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle Jr. said the attack was meticulously planned and jeopardized critical military operations.

"This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism. The defendant allegedly spent months researching the aircraft, acquiring tools and materials and preparing to maximize the destruction he could inflict," Barnacle said.

"The FBI and our law enforcement partners will continue to pursue anyone who targets U.S. military assets, regardless of where those attacks occur."

Severed wiring and damaged components inside a U.S. military C-130H Hercules aircraft after an alleged attack at Shannon Airport in Ireland April 11, 2026, according to federal prosecutors. (Department of Justice)

US EVACUATES 13 MILITARY AIRCRAFT FROM SECOND UK BASE AS NEW IRAN THREAT RAISES ALARM

It remains unclear whether the United States has formally requested O'Corrain's extradition from Ireland. The Justice Department, Irish Department of Justice and Irish prosecutors did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment before publication.

The C-130 Hercules is a four-engine turboprop military transport aircraft used to carry troops, equipment and supplies, including into remote areas with short, rough runways. First introduced in the 1950s, it remains in service today, while the C-130H variant involved in the Shannon Airport incident dates to the 1970s. The aircraft was parked on a taxiway and was due to depart for another country on a U.S. military assignment, according to the indictment.

The indictment outlined how the alleged attack unfolded.

O'Corrain allegedly breached Shannon Airport's security perimeter at approximately 4:40 a.m. on April 11 before crossing the airfield and breaking through the aircraft's rear crew door. Once inside, he barricaded himself using tools and supplies he had brought with him. He also covered the aircraft's windows with the flight crew's hammocks, except for the cockpit windows, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors said he demonstrated detailed knowledge of the aircraft's critical components and how to destroy them while protecting himself. They warned that the aircraft could have been rocked by a massive explosion had O'Corrain cut through its liquid oxygen line instead of pinching it shut.

Five hours later, the flight crew returned to prepare for departure and spotted O'Corrain through a cockpit window, prompting them to alert airport security.

O'Corrain allegedly climbed through a roof hatch and continued damaging the aircraft, striking its exterior with an axe and pouring unidentified substances and placing objects, including ball bearings, into its fuel tanks. Video circulating online at the time appeared to show a man in dark clothing walking along the wing of the aircraft near the engines and fuselage.

Irish police arrived shortly afterward and arrested him.

"These charges send a clear and powerful message that attacks on U.S. military assets — and thus our national security — will not be tolerated," U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said.

Daithi O'Corrain is seen on the exterior of a U.S. military C-130H Hercules aircraft at Shannon Airport in Ireland on April 11, 2026, before his arrest, according to federal prosecutors. (Department of Justice)

Criminal charges in Ireland

O'Corrain is also facing criminal charges in Ireland over the same incident. He was initially denied bail before securing his release through the Irish High Court, according to RTÉ.

Irish prosecutors have since moved to bring the case to trial, with O'Corrain facing charges, including criminal damage to the aircraft and interference with airport operations. He is scheduled to appear in court again in January.

O'Corrain has drawn support from pro-Palestinian activists in Ireland.

An online fundraiser describes him as an independent peace activist and portrays the incident as an act of resistance against the U.S. military's presence in Ireland and American support for Israel. The campaign features a raised fist gripping a hammer — imagery associated with labor and revolutionary movements — superimposed over a photograph of the aircraft.

"An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel’s genocide," organizer Tracey Ryan wrote.

A U.S. military C-130H Hercules aircraft (left) and smashed cockpit instruments (right) after an alleged attack by Irish activist Daithi O'Corrain at Shannon Airport in Ireland April 11, 2026. (Department of Justice)

History of airport breaches

Shannon Airport, which has long served as a transit hub for U.S. military aircraft, was also used by President Donald Trump and Air Force One during his visit to Ireland in September.

The alleged attack followed three other security breaches at Shannon Airport in 2025, according to the indictment. In May, three people were arrested after driving a van through the airport's perimeter fence. Weeks later, three others breached the airfield and sprayed a U.S. military aircraft with paint, temporarily grounding it.

In November 2025, three more people drove a van through the airport's security perimeter and entered a restricted area near a U.S. military C-40 aircraft before being intercepted by security personnel.

Unlike those earlier incidents, the April attack allegedly resulted in the permanent loss of a U.S. military aircraft, with O'Corrain now facing prosecution in two countries.
